The promise of AI automation to fix the administrative problems facing universities is a fallacy. These systems will only increase the burdens of already-struggling institutions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Universities are at a critical point as students and faculty embrace the use of AI. Already, universities like Harvard are introducing courses that feature an AI avatar as an "instructor."

The promises AI offers higher education are familiar: an increase in efficiency as a consequence of less administration, more teaching coverage, better feedback and smarter assessment. But introducing artificial intelligence (AI) systems in an attempt to fix these problems is not the answer. If anything, AI systems will magnify and speed up the bureaucracy that is driving universities' decline.

In practice, the more likely outcome is darker: AI will not simply sweep away the bureaucratic machinery of universities; it will give that machinery a new regime of AI compliance — more policies, more forms, more trackers, more oversight roles and more work downloaded onto faculty who are already stretched thin.

The danger is not that AI will destroy universities but that universities will use AI to preserve the very processes that make them dysfunctional. If this happens, we might see faculty spending less time on research, less time on teaching, and more time on activities that do not directly contribute to the production of knowledge and education of students.

This is already evident in the existing assessment system in the U.K., but shades are creeping into systems elsewhere, providing a window into the future for U.S institutions. A single piece of student work may pass through a plagiarism-detection platform, a grading interface, a moderation spreadsheet for faculty to share feedback, a grade-transfer system, and an exam-board record. Each stage generates its own logins, deadlines, exception rules and audit trails. None of this is inherently malicious. Anonymous marking, moderation, appeals, accessibility and academic integrity are legitimate concerns. But when each concern is implemented as a separate system, the combined effect is administrative incoherence.

In essence, faculty become the human interface between incompatible platforms, spending their time reconciling grades and chasing missing evidence rather than teaching. While this example pertains to U.K. universities, the trend to expand the administrative staff extends to North America. AI simply introduces a new opportunity to increase administration.

AI could, in principle, solve this. It could integrate systems, automate routine reporting, draft feedback, identify inconsistencies and remove duplicate data entry. Yet the institutional incentive is rarely to remove work; it is to make work visible. A university that automates a broken workflow does not necessarily simplify it. It may simply produce faster reports about the broken workflow, more sophisticated dashboards and more elaborate evidence of compliance. The bureaucratic impulse survives by changing its vocabulary: risk management, assurance, transparency, governance, responsible innovation.

At least one possible outcome is that universities will create AI-use policies, require module-level AI statements, mandate disclosure forms, introduce approved-tool lists and establish review committees. Faculty will be asked to redesign assessments, monitor suspected misuse, document their decisions, complete training, and explain their approach to students. Much of this labor will be invisible. It will appear not as a new job title but as an additional expectation attached to teaching.

When something goes wrong, the academic is exposed; when the system works, the institution claims the credit. That asymmetry is corrosive.

That asymmetry is corrosive. It teaches committed staff that careful judgment is not valued as expertise but rather as a compliance risk to be managed, and the consequences will fall unevenly. Experienced faculty, after voicing their concern to no avail, may leave, retire early or disengage. Early-career academics, already precarious because they don't have tenure, will have the least power to resist. Students will receive less of the resource that matters most: sustained intellectual attention.

One possible outcome is that universities will encourage the development of faculty AI avatars and cut hours and employment. The institution will then justify hiring more ‪—‬ not fewer ‪—‬ compliance and "educational enhancement" staff to manage and maintain these AI avatars, negating the idea of efficiency and cost savings. In this scenario, bureaucracy will expand to manage the problems created by its own expansion while undercutting quality for the students who are paying high tuition fees. One might need to hire staff for oversight of these avatars, administrators and lawyers to manage licensing agreements, quality control staff in case things go wrong, and IT teams for integrating them into learning platforms and websites.

There is an alternative to the administrative tasks. AI should be governed by a simple institutional rule: no new compliance requirement without the removal of an equivalent existing burden. If a university requires assessment redesign to accommodate AI, or the introduction of new technology, it should provide protected time, technical support and a single integrated platform. If it expects faculty to manage AI use, it must give them clear institutional backing rather than leaving them to improvise. And critically, it should show how the technology makes work more efficient before rolling it out across the board.

But the deeper issue is not technology but institutional purpose. A university exists — or should exist — to cultivate understanding, judgment and intellectual independence. If its systems consume faculty time, fragment the student experience, and reward documentation over learning, then AI becomes another instrument of managerial self-preservation. The question is not whether universities can adopt AI. It is whether they can resist using AI to automate their own absurdities.

If they cannot, the outcome will be an educational system that looks progressively sophisticated while becoming increasingly hollow ‪—‬ full of monitoring, low on trust; rich in measuring, poor in teaching; obsessed with compliance, indifferent to the people who make education possible; overly procedural sans intellectual life. It will become an audited theater of learning not worth students' time.

Akhil Bhardwaj is an Associate Professor of Strategy and Organization at the University of Bath, UK. He studies extreme events, which range from organizational disasters to radical innovation. Akhil is interested in the epistemological problem of understanding the underlying dynamics that lead up to these events. He also studies how thinking can be improved as well as the implications of AI adoption in the context of strategic management, entrepreneurship, and high-risk systems. His work is philosophically grounded in pragmatism. Prior to joining academia, Akhil has worked as an engineer and manager at CAT., Inc and consulted as a SOX compliance analyst in the U.S.

#6617. Condensed Milk Bread Rolls

Recipe by Kallee Krong-McCreery, Escondido, California

These milk bread rolls are enriched with condensed milk, which makes them fluffy and tender with a touch of sweetness.

Baking bread is one of my biggest culinary joys. It feels magical that a handful of pantry ingredients can create a supple dough, which then transforms into tender, browned bread just begging for a slathering of butter. Whether I’m making sourdough French bread or homemade dinner rolls, the process is mostly the same, but a few small ingredient changes can give a recipe a distinct identity. In these condensed milk bread rolls, that small change is a can of sweetened condensed milk.

This recipe was inspired by Brazilian milk buns (pão de leite condensado) and Portuguese sweet bread, which have sweetened condensed milk added to the dough for flavor and a sugary edge. Most of these recipes use a starter technique called tangzhong, where a cooked flour paste is kneaded into the dough to create a fluffy, cloud-like texture similar to that of Japanese milk bread. We simplified the process for our buns, skipping the starter so they come together without advanced planning.

In a small bowl, dissolve the yeast in warm water. In a large bowl, combine the milk, eggs, butter, sugar, vanilla, salt, yeast mixture and 1-1/2 cups of flour. Beat the mixture on medium speed for three minutes until it’s smooth. Stir in enough of the remaining flour to form a soft dough.

Turn the dough onto a floured surface and knead it until it’s smooth and elastic, six to eight minutes. Place the dough in a greased bowl, turning once to grease the top. Cover the bowl and let the dough rise in a warm place until it has doubled in size, about one hour.

Editor’s Tip: When kneading, start with a light dusting of flour, adding more only as needed. It’s normal for dough enriched with eggs and butter to be tacky initially (it eases as you knead and develop gluten), but adding too much flour will make the bread dry.

Punch down the dough. Turn it out onto a lightly floured surface, then divide and shape it into 12 balls. Place the dough balls in a greased 13×9-inch baking pan. Preheat the oven to 350°. Meanwhile, cover the pan with a kitchen towel and let the rolls rise in a warm place until they have almost doubled in size, 45 to 60 minutes longer.

Editor’s Tip: For evenly-sized rolls, divide the dough by weight using a kitchen scale. The best kitchen scales offer measurements in grams and ounces, so you can divvy up the dough easily no matter which system you prefer.

Bake the rolls until they’re lightly browned, 15 to 20 minutes. Cover the pan loosely with foil if the tops brown too quickly.

Since these rolls are yeast-based and require two rises, you have to make them at least a few hours ahead of time, but you can stretch that to the day before. Make the dough as directed, but cover and refrigerate them after shaping and placing them in the baking dish. The next day, let the rolls warm and rise at room temperature before baking them as directed.

You can freeze baked condensed milk bread rolls for up to three months in an airtight, freezer-proof food storage container. Thaw them in the refrigerator, then warm them in a low oven, around 300°, until they’re soft.

Dense or dry rolls are usually the result of underproofing, overbaking or adding too much flour. Proofing gives the yeast time to lift the heavy dough, weaving air into it for a light texture. If the dough doesn’t rise enough, the lack of air produces rolls with a tight, firm crumb. Use the time cues in this recipe as a guide—proofing may take longer in a chilly kitchen, or go faster on a hot day.

Overbaked rolls can be dry or hard because the extended oven time pulls out their moisture. Since ovens vary, set a timer and check them a few minutes early—even three to four extra minutes can make a big difference. They could also be dry if you knead in too much flour, or if you didn’t measure your flour correctly from the start. Extra flour will hydrate as it proofs, sucking up the liquid that would otherwise contribute to tender rolls.

You can tell yeast is active when a creamy, foamy layer forms on the water’s surface a few minutes after mixing it with warm water. It looks like frothy, milky coffee! Although you don’t always have to proof yeast depending on the type and recipe, proofing active dry yeast gives you visual confirmation that it’s viable. Sometimes the yeast can die off even before the expiration date; proofing checks for that. Once the dough is mixed, you’ll see active yeast at work as it starts to expand, rise and relax the dough.

These lightly sweetened rolls are versatile and can be served for breakfast or brunch with your favorite frittata, crispy bacon and a bowl of fruit salad, or with afternoon tea or dinner. The flavor of the condensed milk—especially as it caramelizes on the roll’s tops—would pair especially well with pork chop dinners, which often feature a sweet ingredient. I also want to try them as a twist on croissant ice cream sandwiches in place of the flaky French pastry.

This recipe doesn’t use a whole can of sweetened condensed milk, but don’t toss the rest. Put it to work in other sweetened condensed milk recipes, or try something new and shake up a Vietnamese coffee martini. Better yet, serve condensed milk rolls with the martini for a happy hour to remember.

#6616. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6615. The Fall Winter 2026 Shoe Trends to Shop Now—From Kitten Heels to Great Boots

Fall’s top shoe trends pick up where we left off in the spring—iterating on classic shapes while infusing them with personality-driven touches. The result? Styles that feel both familiar and new; wearable yet a touch unexpected. And with the spring/summer 2027 collections now unfolding in real time, it’s clear that many of fall’s biggest trends are here to stay.

The kitten heel was a reference point for many designers—Celine, Prada, and Proenza Schouler included—who reworked pared-back silhouettes with playful, feminine flourishes. We’ve seen plenty already on the streets of New York Fashion Week. (Those looking for a little more height can turn to options from Victoria Beckham, Jil Sander, and Stella McCartney.)

Elsewhere, designers reimagined the T-strap—in both heeled sandal and pump form. It’s a perfect transitional shoe—sturdier than a flip-flop, but still perfectly suitable for a warm day. Though, for the colder months, you can pair it with knee-high or crew socks the way Dries Van Noten and Fendi did. Speaking of the colder months, boot season is upon us, and the runways displayed a handful of key silhouettes in that space, including the stretchy sock boot in both knee-high and ankle-height iterations, as well as rugged biker boots.

Slippers made their mark for fall too—from the return of classics like Gucci’s fur-lined horse-bit style to patterned and embroidered takes from Ralph Lauren and Conner Ives. A slip-on brings an ease to daily dressing, adding a polished feel to worn-in jeans and a laid-back cool to skirts. Plus, it’s a welcome flat alternative for party dressing and winter occasions. If heels are more your speed, you’ll find lovely festive options, from Chanel’s two-tone metallic glove pumps to Michael Kors’ red satin square-toed heels—like ornaments for the feet!

Already spotted on the spring summer 2027 runways in New York, kitten heels, textured pumps, and slip-on silhouettes are set to continue their reign. Now is the time to invest in styles that will carry you through the winter and into spring. Below, a closer look at all the top fall/winter 2026 shoe trends.

Don’t miss the rest of our fall/winter 2026 fashion coverage, from the fall fashion trends to know to the handbag styles that complement these looks best.

Biker boots are back in the driver's seat for fall, bringing a rugged, rebellious spirit to even the most feminine looks. At Balenciaga, slouchy black leather boots had a deliberately worn-in attitude, while Dries Van Noten and Proenza Schouler played with the contrast between sturdy footwear and softer, more romantic clothes. For a similar effect, try Balenciaga's buckled motor boots or Dries Van Noten's oxblood leather styles, while Dior's more polished riding-inspired boots offer a sleeker alternative. Frye's classic harness boots and distressed brown suede styles with spurs bring a little Western flair into the mix. Whether you prefer a tall, slouchy silhouette or something shorter and more rugged, these boots are particularly good at toughening up a feminine skirt or dress.

Sleek, streamlined, and endlessly flattering, the sock boot offers a more refined alternative to fall's rugged footwear. At Chanel, pastel-colored boots brought an unexpected softness to eveningwear, while Celine's pointed-toe iterations lent a ladylike finish to romantic skirts. Calvin Klein and Altuzarra favored a more minimalist approach, with supple leather boots that hugged the leg. Celine's glossy black stilettos and Reformation's buttery cream ankle boots capture the silhouette's elegant appeal, while Toteme's burgundy knee-highs introduce a welcome touch of color. For something more understated, Vince's slender black boots and Staud's low-heeled leather ankle style are equally compelling. Whether worn with a midiskirt or tucked beneath tailored trousers, the appeal lies in the silhouette's clean, uninterrupted line.

'Tis the season to put your best foot forward! With holiday invitations piling up, there's no better excuse to indulge in a little festive footwear. On the fall runways, Carolina Herrera and Michael Kors embraced old-Hollywood glamour with elegant evening pumps, while Tory Burch and Ferragamo made a case for shoes with a little extra shine. And why stop at a little? Chanel's crinkled gold leather pumps, Aeyde's silver metallic heels, and Ferragamo's sculptural gold mules are practically made for the dance floor. For a pop of festive red, look to Michael Kors's satin pumps or Aeyde's sleek mules, while Tory Burch's embellished Mary Janes and Herbert Levine's satin heels bring a little whimsy to the occasion. Whether you're dressing for a black-tie affair or cocktails with friends, consider these your invitation to have a little fun from the ankles down.

Fall’s kitten heel marries uptown elegance with downtown edge, thanks to unexpected touches like intricate embellishments and modern hardware. For the on-the-go woman, it’s a sensible style for the 9-to-9—with plenty of personality, to boot.

The slipper’s (or soft loafer, in some instances) effortless yet trend-forward nature was illustrated at Conner Ives and Calvin Klein, where it grounded statement skirts and sequined dresses, respectively. A hybrid of the ballet flat and mule, we love it styled with baggy, wide-leg jeans and a military jacket for an eclectic twist.

The fall/winter 2026 runways went wild for animal print. Leopard, snakeskin, zebra, and even abstract iterations appeared across footwear styles. For the minimalist, take a cue from Khaite and pair snakeskin pumps with rinse-wash denim. Or, for a more maximalist take, look to Isabel Marant, where crimson jeans proved the ideal complement to zebra-print tall boots.

Playing with shape also meant designers revisited the heel itself. The result? Cone heels made their way en masse onto the fall/winter 2026 runways. As seen on pumps, slingbacks, and leather and suede boots, the sculptural silhouette instantly sharpens your look. For right now, reach for a rounded-toe style that slips effortlessly beneath tailored trousers and straight-leg jeans.

A favorite in recent seasons, the fashion pump continues to reign supreme. For fall 2026, fresh takes walked the runway at Stella McCartney, Chanel, and Tory Burch—from barely there glove pumps to pop of color slingbacks. We love it rendered in unexpected hues and playful prints for right now.

The wild card crowdpleaser? Statement shoes! Whether in heeled or flat form, these whimsical creations balance summer’s playful energy with fall’s gravitas. Reach for textured pumps or sequined sneakers to add an unexpected pop to any look. No matter the occasion or destination, they bring a little fancy footwork to every step.

The T-strap makes its return for fall! Dior and Givenchy presented open-toe styles that can easily be added to your transitional rotation. Come later in the season, lean into the trend with a sharp pointed toe and a sock styled underneath. The shape is a natural match for an elegant midiskirt, as seen at Calvin Klein, Dries Van Noten, and Fendi.

#6613. A Classic Thanksgiving Menu With Make-Ahead Tips

The editors at Bon Appétit take Thanksgiving very seriously. People often crave a classic, tried-and-true holiday meal. Guests expect it. So we’re happy to share this menu of Thanksgiving favorites from our archives to get you to the Rockwellian holiday spread of your dreams. These are the dishes we wait all year for: roast turkey and gravy, mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, stuffing, cranberry sauce, buttery rolls, and pumpkin pie. Plus a few tips for making elements ahead.

This recipe, originally published as “Ultra-Creamy Mashed Potatoes” in our 2017 Thanksgiving spread, includes its own list of not-to-miss tips for superior mashed potatoes. The people have spoken: Victoria Granof’s 2012 stuffing recipe gets virtually dog-eared every Thanksgiving. It’s minimalist but has everything you expect from stuffing (technically “dressing” as it’s cooked outside of the turkey in its own casserole dish), including the quintessential quartet of herbs: parsley, sage, rosemary, and thyme.

Making cranberry sauce is the first order of business on my Thanksgiving menu. I usually whip up a batch of Priya Krishna’s 2019 version the weekend before and feel an outsized sense of pride that I’ve managed to tick one thing off the long prep list. Her recipe is a great starting (or ending) point, but you can jazz it up with a cinnamon stick, star anise, or a few cranks of black pepper if you’d like. Or sub in brown sugar for white—the choice is yours!

Try not to fill up on these buttery treasures before The Big Meal. Originally published in the iconic Fannie Farmer Baking Book, we featured these as part of our 2012 Thanksgiving menu in print. You can bake them ahead of time, let them cool, and keep them in the freezer for reheating. Or, if you’re feeling a little adventurous, try their distant cousin, Salt Bread, for even more oohs and ahhs.

Is it even Thanksgiving without pumpkin pie? Rick Martinez’s 2016 rendition is as classic as they come, and it tastes even better the next day (if you’re lucky enough to have any leftovers… come to think of it, maybe just plan on making two?).

You don’t have to cook the whole menu on Thanksgiving morning. Here’s what you can get out of the way:

Remember to account for oven space on Thanksgiving itself: The green bean casserole still needs baking, the stuffing needs its final uncovered bake, and the rolls need warming.

A woman's unexplained abdominal pain led doctors to a diagnosis that has only been documented a few hundred times over the past 400 years.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The patient: A 42-year-old woman in Somaliland, Africa

The symptoms: The woman went to the hospital after having three years of chronic, dull pain in her lower abdomen, as well as a growing sense of heaviness in her abdomen that had worsened in recent months.

When doctors reviewed her medical history, they learned that, three years earlier, she had experienced a number of symptoms that seemed to indicate a pregnancy. She recalled her abdomen growing over time and feeling "fetal movements," her doctors noted in a report of the case. Then, the movements stopped, the abdominal growth halted, and the enlargement gradually subsided. She had not sought medical care during or after this apparent pregnancy.

What happened next: When doctors physically examined the woman's abdomen, they found a hard, irregular mass that extended to her belly button and barely moved when they touched it. Blood tests showed mild anemia, meaning she had fewer healthy red blood cells than normal. Her white blood cell count and kidney and liver tests were normal, and a pregnancy test was negative.

An ultrasound revealed a calcified mass and an empty uterus. Calcification is a buildup of calcium that hardens tissue into a solid mass.

To get a better look at the mass, which occupied the woman's lower abdomen and pelvis, the doctors ordered an advanced CT scan to create a 3D model. The imaging revealed that the mass contained clearly identifiable fetal skeletal structures, including a skull, a spinal column, ribs, and arm and leg bones. The mass measured roughly 7 by 5 inches (18 by 13 centimeters).

The diagnosis: Doctors concluded that the woman had a lithopedion, or "stone baby." The term comes from the Greek words "lithos," meaning stone, and "paidion," meaning child.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a typical pregnancy, an egg is fertilized in a fallopian tube — the structure between the ovaries and the womb — and then travels into the uterus, where it implants in the uterine lining. By contrast, lithopedions most often start as abdominal pregnancies,‬ a type of ectopic pregnancy in which the embryo instead implants on the lining of the abdominal cavity.

There, the embryo shares the space with organs like the stomach, kidneys and appendix. These misplaced pregnancies are almost never viable and are highly life-threatening for the mother. Because the placenta attaches directly to delicate abdominal organs and blood vessels, these carry a severe risk of catastrophic internal bleeding.

If the fetus dies at a developmental stage when it is too large for the mother's body to naturally break down and absorb, her immune system can sometimes treat the retained tissue as a foreign object. To protect the mother from inflammatory complications and infection, the body progressively deposits calcium over the fetal remains, creating a protective casing. In this case, the calcified fetus likely accounted for the woman's chronic abdominal pain and increasing sense of heaviness, her doctors concluded.

The treatment: The doctors performed abdominal surgery to completely remove the calcified fetal mass from the woman's pelvis.

The day after surgery, she developed a mild fever and nausea, but both resolved with treatment. She remained stable and improved during her hospital stay before being discharged in good condition.

Follow-up visits over the next six months showed she had healed well, with a complete resolution of her abdominal pain.

What makes this case unique: Only about 340 cases of lithopedion have been documented in the medical literature over the past 400 years, with the earliest documented in 1582.

This woman's case stands out because she was 42 years old, while many recent cases have been diagnosed in postmenopausal women. (Women typically experience menopause around 51 to 52 years old.) In these cases, the initial ectopic pregnancy occurred during the woman's childbearing years, but she unknowingly carried the calcified remains for decades before developing symptoms. For example, a 74-year old woman from India carried her "stone baby" for more than three decades. By contrast, the woman's recent case was caught after only three years.

The case also highlights the challenges of maternal healthcare in resource-limited settings such as Somaliland, where a lack of access to routine prenatal care and early pregnancy scans can lead to delayed diagnoses. That said, the successful use of advanced 3D imaging and complete surgical recovery demonstrate that excellent outcomes are possible even in these constrained environments, the doctors noted.

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6611. Popeye’s Is Bringing Back This Side Dish for the First Time Since the ’90s

Popeyes is bringing back a nostalgic side dish on Nov. 2, and fans will have plenty to celebrate.

There are two kinds of people in this world: those who go to Popeyes for the chicken and those who will make a special visit just to eat the Cajun fries. Personally, I’m in the second camp. Granted, I have nothing against Popeyes chicken! But the Cajun fries are so deliciously seasoned and perfectly crispy that sometimes I will drive-thru and get them as a snack.

And if you’re also a fan of Popeyes’ side dishes, I have some particularly good news. The Louisiana chicken chain is reaching into its menu archives to bring back a nostalgic favorite that hasn’t been widely available since the ’90s. Let’s just say your next Popeyes order might look a little different!

Popeyes has a long history of serving up more than just fried chicken. When the chain first opened in 1976, its menu featured everything from fried clams to chicken liver. Among those early offerings was a beloved side that eventually disappeared from menus in most markets. But it’s about to make its triumphant return because Popeyes is bringing back Cajun Onion Rings!

The hand-sliced, hand-battered onion rings were slathered with Cajun seasoning. With a distinctive crispy bite, they became a fan favorite almost immediately. In fact, I have family members who constantly compare other fast-food onion ring offerings to the Popeyes version they remember from childhood. In their memories, the Popeyes onion rings were always better!

But the onion rings slowly disappeared from menus. Some locations served them until the 1990s, but by then it was mostly a thing of the past. Now, nearly three decades later, the side dish is finally making its way back.

Onion rings are officially back on the Popeyes lineup now. Availability may vary by location, but this is when you should expect to see them on menus at your local Popeyes.

Priced at $3.99, the Cajun Onion Rings are designed for sharing, although I certainly wouldn’t blame anyone for keeping the whole order to themselves. After all, crispy onion rings are pretty hard to resist. I might even order the onion rings and fries and mix ’em together.

Will you be ordering the new Cajun Onion Rings? Let us know in the comments below!

#6610. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6609. Blanca Miró and Larkspur & Hawk Celebrate Their Colorful Jewelry Collaboration With a Cocktail Party

"I wanted to let the jewelry shine, so I decided to wear something minimal," Blanca Miró told Vogue on Wednesday evening. Minimal, of course, is a relative term. The Barcelona-based designer, known for her exuberant approach to color and pattern, was dressed in head-to-toe orange, accessorized with vintage woven Prada pumps (which she owns in several colorways).

The occasion was a cocktail party celebrating her new collaboration with Larkspur & Hawk, the New York jewelry label founded by Emily Satloff. The two designers, along with their third co-host, writer and tastemaker Tatiana Hambro Arader, gathered friends at Thirty8East, a private art gallery founded by Ashlee Harrison and housed in an Upper East Side townhouse, where an exhibition titled Origins is currently on showcase. On the agenda: a collection of candy-colored rivière necklaces, bracelets, rings, and earrings that marries Miró's playful sensibility with Satloff's fascination with Georgian-era jewelry.

The collection could be spotted around the necks, dangling from the ears, and sparkling on the fingers of guests throughout the room. All three hosts wore the same colorful rivière necklace, though each styled it differently. Satloff paired hers with a vintage floral-jacquard skirt and black high-necked top, while Hambro Arader wore hers backwards, cascading down the open back of a lavender Colleen Allen dress. Three women, one necklace, and three entirely different approaches to getting dressed. Elsewhere, guests including Maria de la Orden, Batsheva Hay, Angelica Hicks, Charlotte Groeneveld, Becky Malinsky Shiah, and Lilly Sisto mingled over Champagne.

The collection features vibrant hues of red, blue, green, and yellow, including a playful take on stripes—a signature of Miró's fashion label La Veste, which she cofounded with Maria de la Orden (who was also in attendance). "What about stripes?" Miró recalled asking Satloff. "Stripes are really hard to do in jewelry," Satloff explained. The solution was to layer strands of different-colored stones, creating a striped effect when worn together.

Other discoveries were more accidental. Satloff recalled experimenting with two different colorways of earrings before pairing them together on a whim. "It was by accident," she said of the resulting mismatched pair. Miró, meanwhile, has become an unlikely earring convert. "I've never really been an earrings person," she admitted. "But since we designed these, I haven't wanted to take them off!"

The two designers' friendship began in 2018, when Satloff spotted Miró wearing one of her necklaces during New York Fashion Week and reached out over Instagram. They corresponded for years before finally meeting in person last year, when they discovered they were wearing nearly identical arrangements of rings. A shared love of antique jewelry, color, and unconventional styling eventually blossomed into the collaboration.

For the celebration, Hambro Arader oversaw the evening's creative direction, arranging the jewels among frosted fruits, silver serving pieces, and colorful textiles. Later, she moderated an informal conversation between the two designers, which touched on their creative upbringings, shared love of antiques, and the historical techniques behind Larkspur & Hawk. Satloff, a former museum curator, explained how she became fascinated by the Georgian practice of placing thin sheets of metallic or colored foil beneath gemstones to enhance their color and luminosity. The foil itself, she explained, was rather like "a candy wrapper" beneath the stone. Which might explain why the finished pieces look so deliciously irresistible!

#6608. What My Job Is Like as a Fact Checker at Bon Appétit

It takes a village to publish a magazine—and website and app and Youtube channel and more. Phew! Today we’re introducing you to Bon Appétit’s research director Ryan Harrington.

For the non-journalists out there: What does research and fact-checking actually mean?

At Bon Appétit, every story or recipe goes through multiple edits. After that, it’s eligible for research review. At that stage, there are a few major things my team and I look out for:

Information accuracy: This includes checking the spelling of names and brands, making sure descriptions of restaurant menus and dishes are up to date, reviewing the credibility of the sources we point to, verifying portrayals of quoted individuals, and anything else to make sure that when you read a Bon Appétit story, you know it’s true.

Cultural sensitivity: For a long time, food media has been dominated by a certain privileged perspective. This perpetuated a system that sort of relived the Age of Explorers, with people “discovering” new foods and pigeonholing or exotifying other cultures. A big part of research is honoring different experiences—giving people a platform without making it a spectacle.

Legal concerns: The research department is a bridge between our actual legal team and the editorial team. We keep an eye out for things like libel issues, copyright infringement, food safety risks, protecting sources, or anything else that might need to be discussed with lawyers.

And for the aspiring journalists: How do you become a fact checker? What did you do before joining the Bon Appétit team?

I finished undergrad with a bachelor’s degree in chemistry and then spent six years managing operations of a thoracic surgery laboratory, studying forms of lung cancer. I reached a point in that career where I was asked to go back to school for a master’s or a PhD. I realized if I were to invest all of my time in further education, I wanted to study something I felt really strongly about. And that was food media.

I entered the NYU Food Studies master’s program with the goal of studying the cultural impacts of food media. Early on, I got an opportunity to intern at Food & Wine. During my time there, I was asked to help with other projects beyond my internship, and that’s when I started thinking about food media not as just an academic subject but as a viable career. I eventually started working for other publications like Travel & Leisure and Lucky Peach (RIP).

I also tried working at a brewery, though I had started there in February 2020. Dealing with the development of COVID was maybe not the best time to dip my toe in the industry, but I did get a better understanding of the pandemic’s impact.

When I saw the research director position at BA, I knew my previous experiences and education gave me a strong skill set to lead research efforts, and I am grateful for the opportunity. I’ve now been here five years.

You also teach food studies at NYU. How does that inform your work at Bon Appetit?

Whether I am building a lesson plan or reviewing a story for BA, I always try to understand things from the perspective of the recipient: the students or readers. Are we conveying the story clearly? What are they taking away from it? Guiding people to those light bulb moments, from the classroom to the newsroom, is why I love doing what I do.

It’s so cool that you started a research fellowship program here, so students can get real-world experience in media. Tell us more about that.

As mentioned, I got my start in the industry thanks to an internship. I never had formal journalism or media training, but it was thanks to that program that I could build relevant experience and make connections that opened up a chain of other opportunities. When I started at BA, it was my top priority in being able to pay it forward and help mentor a new generation of passionate food lovers.

I teach them the skills to be a great research editor and also try to give each fellow the freedom to pursue their own interests and network while here. Some fellows have spent time in our Test Kitchen, seeing how we develop and edit recipes. Some have pitched and written great stories and published them on our site. Some have helped our photo team and learned what it means to style a recipe for a shoot. Every fellow has different ambitions and I want them to get the most out of their time working with us and further their own goals.

What are your favorite types of stories to work on here at Bon Appétit? What are the most challenging?

I grew up watching Alton Brown’s Good Eats. Forever a scientist at heart, this influence had a life-long impact, nurturing a desire to understand not just the “how” but the “why” behind cooking, while simultaneously emphasizing creativity, ingenuity, and understanding. So when we take a deep, explanatory dive in processes, like our video on how Dr. Arielle Johnson makes a chocolate bar, that’s where I really feel like I am in my element. (Fun fact: Arielle and I were chemistry lab partners during our freshman year of college at NYU.)

The biggest challenge for me is when we cover wine. It has a lot of specific terminology, strict regulations across international borders to keep straight, and foreign spellings with diacritics that I have to be mindful of. Thankfully, I have built a contact list of passionate and educated people on the subject that I can consult when I inevitably have questions.

What’s the funniest rabbit hole you fell down on a BA research assignment?

We ran a story featuring Moe Girton and her bar Gossip Grill back in 2021. During her interview, she discussed the lesbian bar scene in San Diego when she first moved there in the late ’90s. There was a note from the author of the story to me: “note to fact-checkers to verify the names [of these bars].”

Of the three bars she mentioned, two were relatively easy to track down and confirm. But that third one did not have much of a digital footprint. I was looking through local newspaper archives, old community forums and message boards, and anywhere else that people might have left mention of this bar. Though I found some clues, sometimes pieces contradicted each other, and eventually I reached back out to Moe to see if she could give me any more info.

While she couldn’t remember too many specifics, I was able to get the cross streets of where she thought it was located. So I called businesses in that area, one by one, to see if: (1) They were around in the late ’90s and (2) They remembered a neighborhood lesbian bar nearby. A long shot, but as luck would have it, I eventually spoke with the owner of George’s Camera, a photography store that has been in business since 1965. Right next door to him used to be Patti’s Bar, a business he described as a “lesbian and biker friendly bar.” And the best part? He happened to have a photo of their storefront from back then, signs and all.

What’s the Bon Appétit recipe you make most often?

I absolutely love Shilpa Uskokovic’s French Onion Tart. It always impresses guests because it seems fancy and labor-intensive, but in reality, it’s so hands-off that I can be doing any number of other tasks (or taking it easy!) while it comes together. The deliciousness-to-effort ROI is through the roof. And two sheets of puff pastry in the box means one for the party, one for breakfast the next morning all to myself.

What’s your favorite obscure food trivia?

I am a product of my time and have spent more than my fair share in debates on “What is a sandwich?” But did you know, in New York, “sandwiches are generally subject to sales tax.” And so, the NY Department of Taxation and Finance has a whole page dedicated to what they consider a sandwich. Spoiler alert: They take a pretty broad stance. Hot dog? Sandwich. Burrito? Sandwich. A freaking buttered bagel? Sandwich.

Other parts of the country hold to a tighter definition. In 2006, the Worcester Superior Court of Massachusetts ruled that a burrito is not a sandwich. When a Qdoba opened in White City Shopping Center, an already present Panera Bread tried to enforce a clause in their lease with the mall that barred any competing sandwich shops from opening. After expert testimony arguing the sides of this case, Judge Jeffrey Locke concluded that a burrito is not a sandwich, allowing Qdoba to operate near Panera without violating the lease.

Maybe there isn’t a perfect answer to this question. Maybe the sandwich was really the friends we made along the way.

Can we convince you to apply to Jeopardy?

The great thing about this job is that I don’t need to know the answer to everything. I just need to know how to find who could answer it. And I don’t think Ken Jennings will let me use Google during filming.

How does AI intersect with or influence your current work?

AI is a powerful tool that can synthesize large volumes of data. But in the world of factual accuracy, there are all sorts of caveats and concerns with the content it generates. It’s still too early to safely adopt blanket applications of AI, but there are ways that it can be useful. Early in my career, when I was the bottom rung of the editorial team, I was often asked to transcribe other reporters’ interview recordings. An hour-long interview could easily take two or three times as long to transcribe by hand with my amateur skills. AI transcription services are far from perfect—and I still need to listen to the recording while reading to verify and fix portions—but it is a huge time-saver.

What kitchen tool (or gadget or appliance) are you obsessed with right now?

I love my immersion blender! It can deal with so many tasks in my lovely but small NYC kitchen without needing any valuable countertop real estate. Pasta sauce, soups, salsa, smoothies, it pureés it all and doesn’t even risk any spillage when trying to move things from pot to pitcher and back to pot again.

Special shout-out to chef Frank Proto’s tip to use a pair of tongs to juice citrus fruits too. Used this one recently while on vacation in the rental home’s bare-bones kitchen. From marinades to margaritas, we needed a lot of fresh squeezed juice and this trick really made things easier.

The movie or TV show you’d rewatch until the end of time?

One of my favorite shows is Happy Endings, a modestly successful sitcom that ran on ABC from 2011–2013. It’s a Seinfeld template of a group of friends navigating urban young adulthood. And like Seinfeld, it has characters that are acutely aware of the social games that they must struggle through to be a part of a functioning society.

I actually wrote an academic paper discussing how Happy Endings explores food and gender through its use (and sometimes subversion) of the big eater trope. It is performed across two characters of different genders and sexuality and represents a convergent idea of exactly that—performance. Society has expectations that can seem limiting or at least arbitrary. But when we see these characters act in ways that challenge these social conventions, it is encouragement for us to be able to do so as well.

#6607. Butterball Made a Tiny Turkey That Assigns Thanksgiving Chores—And It’s Free

Turkey, stuffing and a little accountability are on the menu this year.

There’s always that one Thanksgiving guest who says, “Just tell me what to do!” while somehow managing to avoid doing anything. Well, Butterball has a tiny turkey for that.

On Monday, Nov. 2, the turkey brand took to Instagram to introduce the Butterball Buddy, a tiny electronic taskmaster that hands out Thanksgiving chores so the host doesn’t have to. It looks like something straight out of the ’90s, and the best part? It won’t cost you a dime.

As silly as a chore-assigning turkey sounds, the company might be onto something. Its 2026 Togetherness Report found that 85% of Thanksgiving hosts would prefer guests to offer to help, but only 38% ask. Nearly half say the final cleanup is where they could use an extra hand.

Once everyone arrives, guests pass the Buddy around like a hot potato. When it chimes and vibrates, whoever’s holding it gets a task, whether that’s setting the table before dinner or tackling the dishes afterward. Finish the job, pass it along, and it’s the next lucky helper’s turn. Think Tamagotchi, except instead of keeping a digital pet alive, you’re keeping the kitchen from turning into a disaster area.

Set an alarm. The first batch dropped Nov. 2, and two more are coming at 1 p.m. ET on Monday, Nov. 9, and Monday, Nov. 16, at ButterballBuddy.com. Quantities are limited, so the early birds get the turkey. The giveaway is open to legal U.S. residents ages 18 and older, and no purchase is necessary.

The Buddies may be in short supply, but Butterball’s cooking advice isn’t. Its Turkey Talk-Line is celebrating its 45th anniversary this year, with more than 50 experts answering questions about everything from thawing to checking for doneness through Dec. 24. You can call 1-800-BUTTERBALL, text 844-877-3456 or chat live at Butterball.com. The hotline’s contact information is printed on the back of every Buddy, too.

Who would you hand the Butterball Buddy to first? Let us know in the comments below!

Paleoproteomic analysis of fossils from northern China reveals that Denisovans had a distinctive physical appearance.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The enigmatic and now-extinct Denisovans of China shared traits with Neanderthals, modern humans and Homo erectus, according to a new study that looked at ancient proteins and fossils. But the Denisovans also had several unique skull traits and genetic variants that made them a distinctive ancient human group, according to the researchers ‪—‬ and these traits have now revealed a new face for a Denisovan man.

In the study, published Oct. 21 in the journal Nature, researchers analyzed Denisovan skulls from the archaeological site of Xujiayao in northern China. The Denisovans were a group of ancient humans who lived in Asia and disappeared around 30,000 years ago. This human relative was first identified in 2010 from the DNA of a finger bone discovered in a cave in Siberia.

The Xujiayao bones and teeth were excavated in the late 1970s, long before scientists knew about the existence of Denisovans, and were initially thought to be either Neanderthals or archaic Homo sapiens due to the shape of the fossils and their age: 138,000 to 199,000 years old.

But recent advances in paleoproteomics ‪—‬ the study of bone and tooth proteins that persist longer than DNA ‪—‬ have helped researchers identify Denisovan individuals due to specific genetic variants that differentiate them from other ancient human groups.

In the new study, researchers used paleoproteomic analysis on 20 remains from Xujaiyao and determined that all of them were from Denisovans. This determination then allowed the researchers to study the skull bones closely and figure out what Denisovans might have looked like.

The Xujiayao skulls had some features similar to H. erectus, the researchers wrote, including a low and wide braincase and thick cranial bones. But they also had anatomical features more similar to those of Neanderthals and modern humans, particularly in their bicuspids (the teeth between the canines and molars). The researchers also identified some unique Denisovan cranial traits. The back of the skull, for example, was more vertical and less rounded than in Neanderthals or modern humans.

Armed with a better understanding of Denisovan skull shape from the Xujiayao fossils, the researchers compared them with East Asian Denisovan remains that some experts have assigned to other species, such as Homo juluensis and Homo longi. But the researchers identified similarities that may preclude splitting Denisovans into different species.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"This unique combination of morphological traits, distinct from H. erectus, modern humans and Neanderthal-lineage hominins, supports the assignment of most members of East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo as Denisovans," they wrote in the study. This means that Denisovans may have been one human lineage that adapted to diverse ecological zones across Asia over hundreds of thousands of years.

"It is still possible that there are some other lineages that existed in East Asia during the time Denisovans are known to have existed," study co-author Qiaomei Fu, director of the Ancient DNA Laboratory at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told Live Science in an email.

"We know from DNA that Denisovans were a very varied group genetically, which split early into different populations," Chris Stringer, a paleoanthropologist at the Natural History Museum in London who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email. "These could have developed a lot of morphological variation, which may well surprise us as the sample of fossils grows."

The researchers also produced a new reconstruction of what a Denisovan man might have looked like. A previous DNA study suggested that Denisovans likely had dark skin, brown hair and brown eyes. The new reconstruction shows the Denisovan looking directly at the viewer, with his low, wide braincase mostly obscured by dark hair flowing back from his massive brow ridge. There are clear similarities between the Denisovan man and Neanderthals as well as modern humans, but the Denisovan has a distinct visage all his own.

Xing, S., Wu, Z., Shao, Q., Ge, J., Bennett, E. A., Rao, H., Lin, S., Zhao, Y., Liu, F., Liu, Y., Zhou, K., Feng, X., Jiangzuo, Q., & Fu, Q. (2026). The proteome of Middle Pleistocene Xujiayao and common Denisovan morphology. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11132-z

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6605. Ditch Your Fleet of Coffeemakers—The Chefman Coffee Station Pro Handles Everything

Can't decide between a drip coffee maker, Nespresso, Keurig or an espresso machine? The Chefman Coffee Station Pro does all four—and takes up very little room.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

As Kevin Malone famously said in Season 8, Episode 2 of The Office, “Why waste time say lot word when few word do trick?” In my opinion, the same concept should apply to countertop appliances. After ditching my microwave, countertop oven, air fryer and toaster for the all-encompassing Panasonic HomeChef, I began to wonder what else I could condense into a singular appliance.

After musing over my fleet of five(!!!) coffeemakers consisting of Keurig and Nespresso machines, an automatic espresso maker, a manual espresso maker and a classic drip coffeemaker, I realized that it was time to address the barista elephant in the room. I had to reclaim my coffee bar counter space—but how? The answer, it turns out, is the Chefman Coffee Station Pro.

Here’s how I tested it over several months and why it’s become my go-to coffee machine.

Can't decide on a brew method? The Chefman Coffee Station Pro tackles them all. Yes, really.

In the age of the all-in-one appliance, maximizing countertop space just makes sense. In small kitchens especially, cramming half a dozen different-yet-similar appliances into limited space feels like such a waste. And sure, you don’t need both a blender and a food processor, but it’s nice to have the choice between the two. That’s why combo machines like the Ninja CrushBoss came out and started changing the game. That’s also the idea behind the Chefman Coffee Station Pro.

Unlike other x-in-one machines that incorporate a couple of different brewing methods (looking at you, Keurig K-Duo), the Chefman Coffee Station Pro combines 10 different functionalities into one machine. Craving a quick single cup? You can use it with both K-cups and Nespresso pods. Need to fill up a full carafe for a party? It does that, too. But what if you want to leisurely enjoy an iced latte or a shot of espresso on the weekend? Well, that’s also an option with the built-in manual espresso machine and automatic milk frother.

In terms of functionality, the Chefman Coffee Station Pro offers espresso, cappuccino, latte, single-serve coffee, 12-cup carafe, cold brew, cold-pressed espresso, coffee over ice, hot milk and cold foam. To try it out, I packed up all my other coffee makers and made it my primary coffee machine for two months.

You’d probably expect a machine with so many capabilities to be enormous, heavy, complicated, unwieldily. Not so with the Coffee Station Pro. It’s so simple to set up and use, I didn’t even need to read through the provided booklet before I was whipping up drinks. It also takes up barely more space than a dedicated espresso machine.

Right off the bat, I brewed a pot of drip coffee. First, I’m super impressed with the way the machine can read what I’m brewing based on the basket insert I choose. Pop in the drip basket, and it’s prompting me to choose the number of cups. Swap it out with the K-Cup pod holder, and it’s now asking how many ounces I’d like. It’s truly like magic!

Then, there’s the customization. First, pick between a single cup or a whole carafe. Then, choose to enjoy your coffee either hot or over ice. You also get the option of brewing a cup or a whole pot of cold brew for summertime get-togethers. There’s even a delay brew function, which makes it easy to prep your poison of choice the night before.

As I mentioned, the machine changes its touchscreen prompts based on which brew basket you choose. When you pop in a K-cup, you’re given the option of having it hot or over ice. There’s also a choice of 4-, 6-, 8-, 10- and 12-ounce cups. Then, you can adjust the strength and temperature, with three different settings for each. Finally, there’s a small flip-down platform to rest your cup on so that it doesn’t splash everywhere as it brews.

Want to use a Nespresso capsule instead? A pod insert pops into the K-cup adapter. Again, the machine will intuit this automatically and adjust accordingly. Overall, this aspect of the machine is incredibly intuitive. Plus, you can save specific settings as one of three “favorites,” if you want to speed things up with one-touch operation.

As for espressos, this thing does work. It boasts a 20-bar pressure system that brews espressos topped in a beautiful, silky crema. Pick from a single or double shot, or opt for a cappuccino or latte, both with a choice of single or double. If you choose a milk-based drink, ensure the milk reservoir is filled and angle the metal wand into your cup—the machine does the rest.

If you’re familiar with a standard manual espresso machine, you already know how to operate the portafilter. If not, no worries—there are helpful videos from Chefman to guide you through the process. You can also opt for hot milk, or warm or cold foam on its own by choosing the “froth” setting if you want to add any of those to your cup of regular coffee.

On the top of the machine next to the brew basket is an area with accessory storage for the portafilter baskets, Nespresso adapter and combination scoop/tamper. On the side of the coffee station is a place to stow the portafilter. While there’s no built-in storage for the brew basket, K-cup basket and carafe when they’re not in use, I do love that the smaller accessories have a dedicated space so they won’t be misplaced.

In terms of cleaning, this might be one of the easier machines I’ve ever used. All of the inserts simply rinse clean. But the part I really love is the milk frother. Instead of nooks and crannies that collect smells and residue, the entire thing comes apart into several pieces, so you can thoroughly rinse and wash every single part that touches milk. Win!

Chefman isn’t the only brand to claim that they’ve created an “all-in-one” solution for flexible baristas. In our research, we also found three other similar machines: The De’Longhi All-in-One, the Ninja Prestige Dual Brew Coffee Maker and, of course, the classic  Keurig K-Duo.

The only issue? We couldn’t find a single other appliance that offered K-Cup compatibility and Nespresso pod capability and a carafe and a manual espresso machine and automated milk frothing/latte settings. All of the options above offer at least two functions. Maybe four. But not all five. That crown belongs to the Chefman Coffee Station Pro alone.

Hopefully, we see more options pop up in the near future. But for now, the Chefman Coffee Station Pro is in its own category of coffee maker.

In my home, I used to have five different coffeemakers, including a Keurig, a Nespresso, an automatic espresso machine, a manual espresso maker and a classic drip coffeemaker. In fact, there were so many appliances that they began spilling into my dining room after I ran out of space on my dedicated coffee bar. After converting to the Chefman Coffee Station Pro, I’ve pared that number down to just one. One!

The only changes I’d make after using this machine since August 2026 are minor gripes. I do wish that there was a built-in coffee grinder, since having a separate bean grinder means having yet another appliance. And while I appreciate that there is a small storage cavity for tinier accessories, I don’t love having to find a place in my cupboard for the carafe and basket inserts when I’m not using them.

But honestly? Even with these small annoyances, I wouldn’t even knock off a full star on my final rating. The size, ease of use and cleanliness of the machine make it more than worth it—especially for flexible home baristas like me.

Condense five coffeemakers into just one with this ingenious appliance.

Want to clear up your counter space and join me in the future? You can snag this new appliance on the Chefman website or on Amazon. At $400, the Coffee Station Pro is absolutely an investment. And for some folks who won’t use all the different settings, it may not be worth the cost. But for coffee lovers who want to brew based on vibes (or who already have a long lineup of machines like I used to), the price point feels totally fair. After all, you’re getting five different machines in one!

The easier question is what can’t it make? It’s capable of espresso, single-serve coffee, a 12-cup carafe, cold brew and coffee over ice. While it’s not programmable to make specific drinks such as a cafe crema or Americano like some automatic espresso machines, the manual espresso component and automatic milk frother still offers extreme flexibility for budding baristas.

#6604. Dry-Brined Turkey With Tangy Honey Glaze

This dry-brine turkey recipe produces a Thanksgiving centerpiece that’s full of flavor and juicy as heck. The brine is just kosher salt and brown sugar, applied at least 12 hours and up to 2 days ahead. The salt helps the meat retain moisture, while an uncovered rest in the fridge dries the skin for better browning—no bucket required.

Roasting the bird on a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet (instead of a high-sided roasting pan) lets hot air circulate around it, encouraging browning all over. We’ve also done away with the turkey baster in favor of a buttery honey-vinegar glaze you’ll brush over the bird while it cooks. Fragrant with rosemary, garlic, and orange zest, with Worcestershire sauce for savory depth, the repeated brushing builds an even, glossy lacquer.

Let the cooked turkey rest uncovered for 30 minutes to 1 hour before carving. Resist the urge to tent it with foil, which traps steam and softens that hard-earned crispy skin. Use the downtime to put the finishing touches on your Thanksgiving side dishes.

What kind of turkey should I buy for dry-brining?

Choose an unseasoned turkey. Kosher, self-basting, and enhanced turkeys have already been salted, so adding this dry brine can make them overly salty. Check the label for an added salt solution before buying. A frozen turkey is fine; thaw it in the refrigerator for at least 24 hours before starting the brine.

No. In this recipe, the brine stays on the bird; Step 2 calls for rinsing the baking sheet and rack to prevent the drippings from becoming too salty, not the turkey. Follow the measurement for your brand of kosher salt, and don’t feel compelled to use every last grain of the mixture—the recipe intentionally makes extra.

Yes, but taste them first: The dry brine and glaze make these drippings especially flavorful, and they may be quite salty. Skim off the excess fat to make your roux, then add the juices a little at a time, followed by low-sodium chicken broth (or homemade unseasoned turkey stock).

Our Make-Ahead Gravy doesn’t need drippings, but you can stir some in as it reheats. Taste before adding salt.

Can I use a larger or spatchcocked turkey?

Yes, but not with the same roasting schedule. This dry brine recipe is written for a whole 12–14-lb. bird; a larger turkey or one that’s been flattened will cook differently. For a spatchcocked bird, follow our Spatchcock Turkey With Anise and Orange rather than transferring this recipe’s roasting and glazing times.

See why each step works in our guide to cooking Thanksgiving turkey →

4 hours 45 minutes, plus at least 12 hours brining

Place ½ cup Diamond Crystal or ¼ cup plus 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar in a small bowl and work together with your fingers until incorporated. Place one 12–14-lb. turkey, neck reserved for gravy, giblets discarded, on a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet and pat dry with paper towels. (If you don’t have this setup, place your turkey on a V-shape rack set inside a large roasting pan.) Sprinkle salt mixture all over outside of the turkey as well as inside the cavity of the turkey, patting to adhere and nudging some into every crevice. You won’t need all of the dry brine, but it’s good to have extra since some of it will end up on the baking sheet as you season the turkey. Chill bird, uncovered, at least 12 hours and up to 2 days.

Remove turkey from wire rack and rinse baking sheet and rack if needed (turkey will most likely release some liquid onto pan). Line baking sheet with 3 layers of foil and set rack back inside. Place turkey, breast side up, on rack and tuck wings underneath. Let turkey sit at room temperature 2–3 hours.

Place an oven rack in middle of oven; preheat oven to 450°. Using your fingers, loosen turkey skin on breast. Work 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, under skin, spreading evenly over both breasts. Smear outside of turkey with another 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature.

Tie legs together with kitchen twine and pour 1 cup water into baking sheet.

Roast turkey, rotating pan halfway through, until skin is mostly golden brown all over, about 30 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook ¼ cup sherry vinegar or red wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. honey, 4 tsp. Worcestershire sauce, 3 sprigs rosemary, 3 garlic cloves, crushed, two 2x1" strips orange zest, and remaining 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, in a small saucepan over medium heat until bubbling and slightly thickened, about 5 minutes. Reduce heat to lowest setting and keep glaze warm.

Reduce oven temperature to 300° and continue to roast turkey, brushing with glaze every 30 minutes and adding more water by ½-cupfuls as needed to maintain some liquid in baking sheet, until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of breast near the neck registers 155° (don’t worry; the temperature will continue to climb while the bird rests), 65–85 minutes longer. Skin should be deep golden brown, shiny, and crisp. Transfer turkey to a cutting board and let rest at least 30 minutes and up to 1 hour before carving.

Editor’s note: The dry-brine turkey recipe was first printed in our November 2018 issue as ‘Dry-Rubbed Roast Turkey.’ Head this way for more of our best Thanksgiving recipes →

#6603. Revisiting Jeans and Tees on the Red Carpet, Inspired by the 2027 Met Gala Theme

The 2027 Met Gala theme has officially been announced! Next year, the annual Costume Institute exhibition—titled “extraORDINARY: fashion and the poetics of the everyday”—will ask its visitors “to see the everyday anew,” and will be entirely devoted to celebrating familiar garments and commonplace materials.

The showcase will be separated into two sections: One focused on elevated “archetypal garments,” such as jeans and T-shirts, and the other on garments made of humble and “disposable” materials, including everything from paper to plastic.

While the official 2027 dress code has yet to be announced, it’s an intriguing proposition to strip things back, given the Met red carpets typically lean toward the more extravagant (especially the 2019 Camp year). What can one expect to see celebrities wearing on the iconic Met steps? Jeans and tees will likely have a huge presence on the step and repeat—and past red carpets have proven that A-listers can transform the everyday staples into high-fashion moments.

The simple tee has had many standout moments this year, for starters. Take Zendaya, who rocked a vintage $35 Spider-Man T-shirt earlier this year while promoting her latest installment in the franchise. Wearing it as a dress and pairing it with a pointy white Louboutin pump? Instant fashion serve. Further back in 1999, Liv Tyler and Stella McCartney also both hit the Met Gala in matching “Rock Royalty” tees—turning the simple graphic top into a bold, cheeky statement. You can get abstract with it, too: Charli XCX’s 2024 Met Gala gown, by Marni, was made of patchworked T-shirts.

Jeans, too, have been elevated and transformed on the red carpets. This year, model Bhavitha Mandava wore Mathieu Blazy’s Chanel—her beige muslin half-zip sweater worn over a pair of muslin-printed pants that had a blue jean effect. A fancy-fied, couture jean! Troye Sivan also wore head-to-toe Prada, including a light-wash pair of jeans that served as an homage to the artist Robert Mapplethorpe and his distinct personal style. Jeans, it turns out, can have just as much of a dramatic effect as a ball skirt or suit trouser; It’s all in the storytelling and styling approach.

So, will the 2027 Met Gala unearth some unexpectedly chic jeans and tees moments? You can definitely count it. And if celebrities need some inspiration, fear not: Below, revisit even more of the best jeans and tees moments on the red carpets over the years.

Delight your favorite foodie with a full fleet of flavors when you gift them an Enzo Olive Oil gift set!
